newsitem.title: USA: Clinton administration defends gun-control law.
newsitem.headline: Clinton administration defends gun-control law.

text.p: A top Clinton administration lawyer defended the historic, hard-won Brady gun-control law before the U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday against opponents who argue that it is unconstitutional.

During arguments on the law, which sparked a political battle before Congress approved it and President Bill Clinton signed it in 1993, Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger urged the court to uphold its requirement that local sheriffs run background checks on prospective handgun buyers.

The law is the first successful effort by Congress in 25 years to regulate firearms in a country in which there are more than 100 million guns in private hands and a powerful political lobby to allow unrestricted gun ownership.
It was named after former White House Press Secretary James Brady, who was wounded and permanently disabled in the 1981 assassination attempt on President Ronald Reagan.

Dellinger said the local checks for any record of crimes, mental illness, drug use or other disqualifying problems -- done during a five-day waiting period before a gun sale can be completed -- are required only as an interim measure until a national system goes into effect in late 1998.

Dellinger, who as solicitor general is the administration's chief advocate before the Supreme Court, said Congress decided against waiting for the federal system to take effect because "there are 1,300 handgun murders a year."

Lawyer Stephen Halbrook, representing two sheriffs from Arizona and Montana who brought the court challenge, said the law wrongly forces police to carry out a federal programme. "These commands are not constitutional," Halbrook said.
The justices questioned both lawyers vigorously during the hour-long arguments, especially on how far Congress may go in extending the reach of federal power over the states.
The high court's decision is expected by the summer.
Brady and his wife, Sarah, who have become leading gun control advocates, were in the packed courtroom as was one of the plaintiffs, Sheriff Jay Printz of Montana.

Justice Stephen Breyer asked what was wrong with using local sheriffs instead of relying on federal agents to make the background checks. He said that in some European nations it would show more "respect" to localities to impose minor duties on them rather than creating a new federal bureaucracy.
Halbrook said Congress lacks the power to adopt a law that forces states or local governments to provide records to the federal government.
"That's an extreme position," said Justice Sandra Day O'Connor.

She later asked if the constitutional problems would disappear if Congress had offered money to the local governments to conduct the checks, or made them optional. "There was no money and no option," Halbrook replied.
Dellinger said the checks had to be mandatory because if just one county announced it would not do them, "that's the county where felons will buy the guns."
But his argument that the law does not force sheriffs to make policy choices met with scepticism from several justices.
Clinton said on Monday he believes the law passes constitutional muster and has saved many lives.
